study_identification.title: Individual deviations from normative models of brain structure in a large cross-sectional schizophrenia cohort

study_characteristics.study_objective: To map deviations from normative ranges of brain structure for individual patients with schizophrenia and evaluate whether the loci of individual deviations recapitulated group-average brain maps of schizophrenia pathology. Additionally, to explore potential genetic and clinical drivers of such deviations.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FSL 5.11 (diffusion tensor fitting, eddy current correction); ANTs (spatial normalization); Freesurfer 6.0 (cortical thickness estimation); ICBM-DTI-81 white matter atlas (48 tracts); Desikan-Killiany atlas (68 cortical regions)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Participants showing gross artifacts, cerebellar cropping and/or significant head motion were excluded following established protocols. Six individuals with schizophrenia were excluded due to artifacts (movement, ghosting and/or signal dropout). Supplementary analyses showed that the AAI did not associate with absolute (r = -0.031, p = 0.6) or relative (r = -0.049, p = 0.41) head motion estimates in diffusion MRI.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Multi-level harmonization strategy: (1) Pre-data collection: inter-site calibration using traveling subject scanned at all five sites and Siemens MRI phantom at each site; (2) Post-acquisition: retrospective harmonization of diffusion-weighted images using nonlinear mapping based on rotation invariant spherical harmonics features, with Brisbane as reference site and age/sex-matched healthy controls from remaining sites. Site was also included as nuisance confound in quantile regression models.

response_variable.answer: Tract-averaged fractional anisotropy (FA) across 48 white matter tracts; Cortical thickness (CT) across 68 cortical regions (Desikan-Killiany atlas)

predictor_effects.answer: Age: fixed effect (linear); Age-squared: fixed effect (included only when justified by Bayesian Information Criterion for nonlinear age effects); Sex: fixed effect; Sex-by-age interaction: fixed effect (included only when justified by BIC); Site: nuisance confound (treated as fixed effect). The model was centered at average age of the healthy control group.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study implements multiple strategies to handle nuisance structure: (1) Site effects are explicitly modeled as nuisance confounds (Ci) in the quantile regression model; (2) Nonlinear age effects are accommodated via age-squared term when justified by BIC; (3) Sex-by-age interaction is included when justified; (4) Multi-level harmonization was performed including pre-collection calibration and post-acquisition retrospective harmonization of diffusion images using nonlinear mapping; (5) Heteroscedasticity is inherently handled through quantile regression which estimates conditional quantiles rather than means. The study also verified that head motion (a source of measurement error) did not associate with deviation metrics.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: For the healthy participant with index i, sex_i encodes the participant's sex (male: 0, female: 1), age_i is the participant's age, and C_i encapsulates nuisance confounds, including acquisition site. ... β_3 and β_4 model the sex-by-age interaction and nonlinear age effects, respectively. The sex-by-age interaction (β_3) and the nonlinear age-squared term (β_4) were only included when justified by the Bayesian information criteria. ... An individual traveled to all five sites and was scanned at each site to quantify gross inter-site differences. A Siemens MRI phantom was also scanned at each site to enable inter-site calibration. This calibration was done prior the data collection to help minimize the inter-site variability caused by the scanner. In addition, in this study, the diffusion-weighted images were retrospectively harmonized to alleviate possible nonlinear site-related differences. We followed a robust harmonization procedure developed in our previous work.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Materials and methods section, Harmonization and Normative modeling subsections (lines 66-93 in main text)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The paper does not report validation metrics on the training data itself, such as examining model residuals, goodness-of-fit statistics, or deviation score distributions on the healthy controls used to train the model. While model selection used BIC, this is for comparing model complexity rather than validating model fit on training data.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Not applicable - no training set validation reported.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study employed rigorous 10-fold cross-validation on independent healthy control data. Percentile curves were fitted on n=175 training subjects and tested on n=20 held-out subjects, repeated 20 times with random test-training splits. The validation criterion was that >90% of test-set healthy controls should fall within the 5-95% normative range. All regions and tracts met this criterion, confirming the model does not over-predict deviations.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: To this end, percentile curves were fitted using a randomly selected subset of healthy individuals (n = 175, training set) and the proportion of remaining healthy individuals residing within the 5–95% percentiles (normative range) was enumerated (n = 20, test set). This was repeated for 20 randomly selected test-training subsets, using a tenfold cross-validation framework. For all cortical regions and white matter tracts, more than 90% of the healthy individuals in each test set resided within the normative range (Supplementary Fig. 3), confirming that the normative models were not predicting an excessive number of deviations (i.e., no fewer than 90% of healthy individuals should reside within the normative range defined by 5–95% percentiles).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Results section, Individual deviation from normative range subsection (lines 122-128)

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study conducted site-wise reproducibility analyses by computing deviation maps independently for each of the five acquisition sites and evaluating spatial correlation across sites. This represents a form of leave-one-site-out external validation within the multi-site cohort. Infra-normal CT maps were significantly correlated between most site pairs (r = 0.25-0.6, p < 0.05 for 10/11 pairs), and FA maps were correlated for most pairs except those involving the two smallest sites (Perth n=37, Newcastle n=17). However, this is not validation on a completely independent external dataset from a different study/cohort, but rather cross-site validation within the same multi-site study. The harmonization and site-covariate modeling may have facilitated this cross-site consistency.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Control analyses were undertaken to evaluate the reproducibility between acquisition sites (Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Perth, Newcastle) in the cortical maps expressing the percentage of individuals with infra-normal deviations (Fig. 2c, d). To this end, infra-normal maps were computed independently for each site and the spatial correlation across cortical regions in the percentage of individuals with infra-normal deviations was evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient. Infra-normal CT maps were significantly correlated between all 11 pairs of sites (r = 0.25–0.6, p < 0.05), except for the Sydney-Newcastle pair (Supplementary Fig. 6). Infra-normal FA maps were significantly correlated for all pairs, except for pairs involving Perth and Sydney (Supplementary Fig. 7). Cohort sizes were smallest for Perth (n = 37) and Newcastle (n = 17), potentially explaining the lower reproducibility for these two sites.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Results section, Reproducibility between acquisition sites subsection (lines 164-178)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores from 5th and 95th percentiles (derived from bootstrapped confidence intervals). Infra-normal: z_5 < -1.96 (below 5% confidence interval for 5th percentile); Supra-normal: z_95 > 1.96 (above 95% confidence interval for 95th percentile); Normal: within 5-95% percentile range. Average Abnormality Index (AAI): whole-brain summary computed as mean of encoded deviations (+1 for supra-normal, 0 for normal, -1 for infra-normal) across all 116 loci.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Pearson correlation between polygenic risk score (PRS) and AAI indices (overall, CT-only, FA-only), with age/sex/site regressed from raw measures. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to identify multivariate associations between: (1) deviation scores (116 regions/tracts) and PRS; (2) deviation scores and four symptom dimensions from ICA (cognitive performance, hallucinations, depressive symptoms, negative symptoms). Permutation testing (5000 permutations) with family-wise error control for CCA. Supplementary univariate analyses: two-sample t-tests comparing each DIP item between infra-normal vs. normal/supra-normal groups for each region (FDR < 5%). Cross-validation framework for group differences. Correlation between CT and FA AAI indices. Correlations between AAI and current IQ.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Anatomical loci of schizophrenia-related brain changes are highly heterogeneous across individuals to the extent that group-consensus pathological maps are not representative of most individual patients, despite widespread group-level reductions in FA and CT.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Group-level analyses revealed widespread reductions in FA and CT in schizophrenia (83% of 48 tracts, 88% of 68 regions, FDR < 5%). However, normative modeling showed profound individual heterogeneity: no more than 15-20% of patients deviated from normative range for any single tract or region. Despite this, 79% of patients showed at least one infra-normal deviation (vs. 59±2% of healthy controls, p < 0.001), while only 46% showed at least one supra-normal deviation (vs. 61±3% controls, p < 0.001). Higher polygenic risk for schizophrenia associated with greater number of infra-normal CT deviations (AAI overall: r = -0.13, p = 0.033; CT-only AAI: r = -0.17, p = 0.006), explaining 1.8-3% variance. CCA identified significant mode linking PRS to regional deviations (r = 0.69, p = 0.044), with infra-normal CT in temporal regions as strongest predictors. PRS did not correlate with raw FA/CT measures. CT and FA AAI were significantly correlated (r = 0.26, p < 0.001), suggesting linked gray-white matter pathology. Marginal CCA association found between symptom dimensions and deviations (r = 0.75, p = 0.048). Specific DIP items (hallucinations, delusions, depression) associated with CT deviations in frontal/temporal regions (FDR < 5%). Current IQ correlated with CT AAI (r = 0.16, p = 0.008) but not FA AAI. Results replicated with higher-resolution Destrieux atlas (148 regions), showing high correlation between atlases.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: MRI data inherently noisy and individual measurements susceptible to noise/artifacts, though mitigated by: identical acquisition sequences/scanners across sites, robust measures, averaging over large numbers of voxels/vertices, and quality control exclusions. Harmonization performed for FA but not structural MRI; deviation maps not reproduced for two smallest sites (Newcastle, Perth). Normative range operationalized subjectively (5-95% percentiles); further work needed to determine clinically meaningful thresholds. Larger normative samples would refine ranges and confidence intervals but may introduce harmonization challenges. Individual variation in medication status, age of onset, illness duration could contribute to heterogeneity. Alternative normative modeling techniques (moving averages, machine learning) should be considered for larger samples. Diffusion data acquired on 1.5T scanners with single-shell sequence, limiting investigation of specific microstructural properties beyond conventional anisotropy. Difficult to differentiate IQ effects from disorder itself given pervasive cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Normative models provide a way forward to unravel neuropathological heterogeneity and potentially facilitate personalized medicine in neuropsychiatry. Individual deviation maps could be used to: (1) identify personalized targets for neural stimulation therapies; (2) enable patient-centered approaches to selection of antipsychotic drugs; (3) delineate putative subtypes. The study calls into question the viability of ongoing endeavors to derive group-average network and cortical maps of schizophrenia pathology using conventional case-control paradigms.

general_notes.general_notes: This study demonstrates that while schizophrenia shows widespread group-level brain abnormalities affecting virtually all regions, the specific anatomical loci affected vary markedly between individuals. The findings suggest that pooling heterogeneous subtypes yields diffuse group-average maps that may not accurately represent individual patients. Multi-site study with five Australian sites using identical Siemens Avanto scanners and acquisition protocols. Genetic data: 112 of 128 genome-wide significant SNPs used for PRS (16 excluded due to >20% missingness or imputation QC failure). Clinical assessment domains included DIP, SANS, WASI, RBANS, COWAT, reduced to four ICA dimensions. Quantile regression with bootstrapping (n=1000) used to estimate confidence intervals for percentiles. Supplementary analyses showed robustness: results replicated with Destrieux atlas (148 regions); CT-FA deviations correlated; reproducibility across most site pairs. The average abnormality index provides individual-level summary but CCA revealed regional specificity (temporal cortex most implicated). Study represents important methodological advance in parsing heterogeneity beyond group-average approaches.
